chapter: Chapter II: The Immortality of the Soul (Atman)
text: Never the spirit was born; the spirit shall cease to be never; Never was time it was not; End and Beginning are dreams! Birthless and deathless and changeless remaineth the spirit for ever; Death hath not touched it at all, dead though the house of it seems! As a man casteth off worn-out garments and putteth on others that are new, even so the embodied soul casteth off worn-out bodies and entereth into others that are new. Weapons cleave it not, fire burneth it not, water wetteth it not, wind drieth it not away. For the Soul is eternal, all-pervading, unmoving, and everlasting.

chapter: Chapter II: Nishkama Karma (Action Without Attachment)
text: Thy right is to the work alone, but never to its fruits; let not the fruit of action be thy motive, nor let there be in thee any attachment to inaction. Perform action, dwelling in devotion, abandoning attachment, and remaining balanced in success and failure; for equanimity of mind is called Yoga. Far lower than the Yoga of wisdom is mere selfish action; seek refuge in selfless understanding, for wretched are they who labor merely for the rewards of their deeds.

chapter: Chapter II: The Sage of Steadfast Wisdom (Sthitaprajna)
text: When a man puts away all desires of the heart, and is satisfied in the Self alone by the Self, then is he called a person of settled wisdom. He whose heart is not shaken amidst afflictions, who in pleasures is free from craving, from whom passion, fear, and anger have fled away, he is called a sage of steadfast mind. Even as the tortoise draws in its limbs from all sides, when a person withdraws his senses from sense-objects, his understanding is firmly poised in tranquility.

chapter: Chapter III: The Necessity of Pure Action (Karma)
text: None can remain even for a moment without performing action; for everyone is helplessly driven to act by the qualities of nature (Gunas). He who restrains his organs of action while his mind dwells on the objects of desire is a hypocrite. But he who, subduing the senses by the mind, undertakes Karma Yoga without attachment, he excels. Perform thy allotted duty, for action is far superior to inaction; even the preservation of thy physical life cannot be achieved without action.

chapter: Chapter IV: The Fire of Wisdom (Jnana Yoga)
text: Even as a blazing fire burns its fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of wisdom burn all karma to ashes. There is no purifier in this world like spiritual wisdom. He that hath faith and hath conquered his senses gains this wisdom; and having gained wisdom, he quickly attains supreme peace. He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is a yogi who accomplishes all true work.

chapter: Chapter VI: The Self as Friend and Enemy
text: Let a man lift himself by his own Self, let him not degrade himself; for the Self alone is the friend of oneself, and the Self alone is the enemy of oneself. The Self is a friend to him who has conquered himself by the Self; but for him who is undisciplined, his own self acts like a hostile adversary. In the serenity of self-mastery, the supreme Self abides unwavering in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honor and disgrace.

Better is one's own duty (Svadharma), though imperfectly performed, than the duty of another well performed. Surrendering all actions unto the Supreme, fixing the mind on the Eternal, free from self-interest, egoism, and anxiety, engage in the battle of life. The soul that acts without selfish attachment, consecrating every deed as a sacrifice for universal welfare (Lokasangraha), is untouched by sin, even as a lotus leaf remains unwetted by water.
